why: A thrashing agent looks identical to a working one in its own pane and no harness flags it, so catching it means re-reading several panes over time and remembering what they said before - genuinely a correlation-over-time job. Impact is real because the action is concrete and immediate (kill or redirect), and the loss avoided is measurable quota and wall-clock, not just curiosity. Marked down slightly because a detector will misfire and users learn to distrust it.

The ranking itself is derivable only after you know every session state, which is the cross-session work no harness does; but it is a sort applied to information, not new information. Impact is where it collapses: with 3-12 sessions the number actually waiting on you at any moment is one or two, and once you can see which those are, ordering them changes almost nothing. A queue is a nicety layered on the needs-input signal.

The user opened the tabs; the count is roughly in their head and fully confirmable by glancing at the tab bar or one tmux list-panes. Impact is self-admittedly nil - no decision hangs on the integer. This is dashboard furniture, the kind of tile that looks like a metric and is really a headcount.

As an action it is doable by hand today - commission a workflow and re-brief the agent - just tedious, so it is annoyance not impossibility. Impact is narrow: it presupposes the user already runs Spacedock and wants a first officer, which describes a sliver of the audience, and for everyone else the promote button is dead weight. Convenience for an existing power user, not a new capability.

A dead session is one of the easier things to check unaided - the pane shows the crash or shell prompt, and ps confirms it - but you have to visit the pane, so it hides until you look. Impact is decent: waiting on a corpse is pure dead time and the response (restart) is unambiguous. Held under 60 because the loss is minutes of idle waiting, and users usually discover it on their next sweep anyway.

Claude Code already ships a usage command that reports quota, and per-model breakdown is precisely the kind of thing the vendor owns and keeps improving - one command away today, commodity within a year. Impact survives better than access: switching Opus to Sonnet instead of downing tools is a genuine behaviour change that keeps work moving, and it recurs weekly for heavy users.

Producing a hand-off is one prompt to the agent you are already talking to, and harnesses already ship compaction and session resume, so this is mildly annoying rather than unreachable and is a strong candidate for native commoditisation. Impact is moderate: it saves re-briefing effort, but the wall is not usually a surprise and the recovery cost without it is minutes of re-explaining, not lost work.

Nothing surfaces a token rate over time, and reconstructing one means parsing transcripts, so it is genuinely hard to obtain by hand. That earns it nothing, because the item itself concedes no decision follows: a sparkline that is high or low does not tell the user to do anything different. Classic high-access, zero-impact ornament - impressive to build, ignored after week one.

Comparing the stated plan against the actual diff means reading back through a transcript and running git diff per session - reachable, but nobody does it across a dozen sessions, so effectively a correlation task. Impact is weaker than it sounds: the diff gets reviewed at commit or PR time anyway, that review is the real backstop, and an automated drift claim will be noisy enough that users stop acting on it.

Any single session shows its own prompt on screen, so this is not unobtainable - but you only learn it by being in that pane, and across 3-12 panes discovery degrades to periodic manual sweeps that people do late or not at all. Impact is the highest here: a blocked agent burns wall-clock doing nothing until noticed, the fix is one keystroke, and it recurs many times a day. This is the load-bearing signal the rest of the board leans on.
